title: US Economy Grows at Fastest Pace in a Year, but Voters Aren't Feeling It
excerpt: GDP rose 3.4% in the third quarter on consumer spending and an AI investment surge, while 62% of voters in a Journal poll rated the economy not so good or poor.
body:
• US GDP grew at a 3.4% annual rate in the third quarter, the fastest pace in a year, the Commerce Department reported last week — yet a Wall Street Journal poll last month found 62% of voters rated the economy not so good or poor.
  • Consumer spending rose at a 3.8% annual rate for a second straight quarter, and a measure of private demand grew 4.9%, its best since 2021, the Journal reported.
  • Reuters reported business spending on equipment surged 20.9%, the fastest since 2020, driven by artificial intelligence investment.
  • The split lands two days before the midterms: for Indian-American voters, the cost of living — not the GDP print — is the number campaigns are fighting over.

The US economy is accelerating. Gross domestic product grew at a 3.4% annual rate in the third quarter, its fastest pace in a year, and consumer spending — the largest contributor — rose at a 3.8% rate for the second quarter in a row, The Wall Street Journal reported. A closely watched measure of private demand grew even faster, at 4.9%, its best performance since 2021.

And yet voters are not feeling it. In a Wall Street Journal poll conducted last month, 62% of respondents rated the economy not so good or poor, against 37% who rated it good or excellent. The same poll showed 51% of registered voters expecting to vote Democratic, versus 44% for Republicans.

"The economy is robust, but it is also extremely concentrated."

— Gregory Daco, EY-Parthenon economist, quoted by The Wall Street Journal

Growth with a narrow base

The Journal's account is of an expansion powered by the artificial intelligence boom and robust consumer spending, strong enough to push through wars, volatile markets and trade disruptions — but unevenly shared. Higher borrowing costs have grown alongside profits and wealth, and while wages have risen, inflation has eaten most of the gains.

Reuters reported the same Commerce Department release from a different angle: business spending on equipment surged at a 20.9% rate, the fastest since the third quarter of 2020, adding 1.16 percentage points to GDP growth. Spending on intellectual property products grew 8.4%, mostly software and research and development. Economists polled by Reuters had forecast 3.2% growth; the economy beat that, accelerating from 2.2% in the second quarter.

The September soft spot

The quarter ended less strongly than it ran. Separate Commerce Department figures showed inflation-adjusted consumer spending was flat in September from a month earlier, the Journal reported. Over the 12 months to September, real consumer spending rose 2.5%, but real after-tax personal income grew only 1% — a gap households have been filling from savings. Barclays economist Jonathan Millar told the Journal the economy is in good shape, though perhaps not quite as robust as the third-quarter figures suggest.

Why it matters on Tuesday

The GDP report arrived less than a week before the November 3 midterms, which will decide control of Congress. A forecasting model by Yale economist Ray Fair, cited by the Journal, puts Democrats at about 50.6% of the two-party House vote on the latest data. The political puzzle is the one in the headline: an economy can post its fastest growth in a year while most voters rate it poorly, because what voters experience is prices and borrowing costs, not output statistics. Despite a weak past month on AI-risk worries, the S&P 500 closed Friday up 11% from the end of last year — another number that describes portfolios better than grocery bills.
